Family Health

Depression around menopause: symptoms and treatment choices

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Mood can change around menopause, but persistent depression deserves its own assessment and treatment. Hormonal changes, sleep problems, previous depression and life pressures can interact. You do not have to wait for your periods to stop, or assume that hormones alone explain how you feel, before asking for help.

Menopause, perimenopause and mood are not the same thing

Perimenopause is the transition leading to menopause. Periods may become more or less frequent, heavier or lighter. Natural menopause is usually recognised after 12 months without a period, when another cause does not explain it; hormonal contraception can obscure this pattern. The transition often begins in the forties but timing varies.

Some people experience mood swings, anxiety or low mood, while others develop a depressive disorder. Depression is not inevitable, a character weakness or simply an expected part of ageing. It can start before, during or after menopause, and needs attention even when hot flushes are absent.

Hormones, sleep and life pressures can interact

Changing reproductive hormones can affect brain systems involved in mood, including serotonin signalling, but depression is not explained by a single falling hormone or a simple shortage of a happiness chemical. Biological, psychological and social factors contribute. Hormone-sensitive periods, including menstrual changes, pregnancy and the postpartum period, can be vulnerable times for some people, not everyone.

Night sweats and insomnia can worsen tiredness, irritability and mood; depression can also disturb sleep. There is no universal tenfold risk from poor sleep. Caring for ageing parents, work demands, health concerns, relationship changes or children leaving home may add pressure. A previous depressive episode is a reason to plan support and watch for returning symptoms, not a certainty of relapse.

Recognise symptoms and seek an assessment

Possible symptoms include persistent sadness, hopelessness or irritability, losing interest or pleasure, low energy and motivation, changes in appetite in either direction, sleeping too little or too much, and trouble concentrating, remembering or making decisions. Thoughts about death, suicide or self-harm always deserve prompt attention. Not everyone has every symptom.

Arrange a clinical appointment if mood affects work, study, relationships or everyday activities, or symptoms persist most days for about two weeks. Seek help sooner if severe or worsening. Discuss periods, sleep, hot flushes, previous mental health problems, medicines, alcohol and life stresses. Assessment considers duration, impact, safety and other possible causes; a symptom checklist or hormone result alone cannot diagnose depression.

Talking therapy and antidepressants: a personal plan

Psychological treatment such as cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) can help with depression. Menopause-specific CBT can also help some menopause-related low mood, hot-flush distress or sleep problems. These uses overlap but are not identical. For less severe depression, supported self-help or psychological approaches may be appropriate; antidepressants are not automatically the first option unless they are your informed preference.

For more severe or recurrent depression, antidepressants, individual therapy or a combination may be considered. CBT plus medication can be useful, but it is not invariably the best choice for everyone. Antidepressants are not reserved only for people who decline HRT. Agree on expected benefits, side effects, interactions, early follow-up and a relapse plan. Do not start, change or abruptly stop medication without the prescriber’s advice.

Where hormone replacement therapy fits

HRT treats menopause symptoms and may be considered for depressive symptoms that began alongside other menopause symptoms but do not meet criteria for depression. If depression is suspected or diagnosed, use depression care alongside appropriate menopause management. HRT is not a default substitute for depression treatment or a guaranteed antidepressant.

Systemic oestrogen may be given as a patch, gel, spray or tablet. People who have a uterus usually also need progestogen to protect its lining; the regimen depends on menstrual stage and history. HRT can be used after menopause when appropriate: being postmenopausal is not itself a prohibition. Discuss personal benefits, risks and review arrangements rather than copying another person’s prescription.

HRT and the combined contraceptive pill have different risks

Smoking, blood pressure, clotting history, cancer history and liver disease need a careful review. Smoking is a reason for risk assessment and stopping support, not an automatic rule that every HRT form is forbidden. Uncontrolled high blood pressure should be treated before HRT; controlled blood pressure does not automatically exclude it. Previous clots require individualized, often specialist advice; tablets and skin-delivered HRT have different clot risks. A patch does not remove every risk or make self-prescribing safe.

A combined contraceptive pill may suit selected people during perimenopause who also need contraception, but it is different from HRT and is not a general depression treatment. Smoking at age 35 or older, hypertension and a history of clots can make combined hormonal contraception unsuitable. HRT itself does not prevent pregnancy. Discuss a safe contraceptive and symptom-management plan rather than switching or combining hormones yourself.

Daily support and recovery after menopause

Regular meals, enjoyable activity, a manageable sleep routine and practical or social support can help wellbeing alongside treatment. Reducing caffeine if it worsens sleep or flushes, limiting alcohol and getting help to stop smoking may be useful. These steps are not a test of willpower or a replacement for care when depression is significant. Discuss supplements or herbal products before using them because interactions and uncertain safety matter.

Some symptoms improve as the transition settles, but depression may persist or recur after menopause. Recovery cannot be predicted simply from the final period or hormone stability. Keep follow-up appointments, review response and side effects, and agree what to do if symptoms return. You can ask for changes to a plan that is not helping; effective treatment sometimes takes adjustment.

When help is urgent

Seek urgent professional help for suicidal or self-harm thoughts, even without a plan. If you may act on them, cannot stay safe, or have already seriously harmed yourself or taken an overdose, contact local emergency services or go to an emergency department immediately. Tell a trusted person and ask them to stay with you while help is arranged. Do not wait for a routine menopause appointment.

New or worsening agitation, marked mood changes or suicidal thoughts after starting or changing treatment need prompt contact with the treating team; immediate danger requires emergency help. A clinician can arrange more support and review treatment. Asking about safety is a normal part of care, and depression remains treatable even when symptoms are severe.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

NICE menopause guidance, updated April 2026, distinguishes menopause-associated depressive symptoms from diagnosed depression and recommends coordinated care.

NICE adult depression guidance supports assessment and shared treatment choices, including psychological therapy and appropriate medication, with safety monitoring.

NHS advice separates HRT from contraception and supports individual review of blood pressure, clot risks, sleep and daily support.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to note mood, sleep, period changes and questions for appointments. It cannot diagnose depression, assess suicide risk or decide whether hormones or medicines are safe for you; seek professional help according to your symptoms.

When to seek help

Seek urgent help for suicidal or self-harm thoughts. Immediate danger, inability to stay safe, serious self-harm or overdose requires emergency services or an emergency department now. Do not wait for a menopause visit or change prescribed medicines yourself.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Depression around menopause is treatable and is not inevitable or your fault.
  • Persistent symptoms, functional difficulties or returning depression need assessment; safety concerns need help sooner.
  • CBT, antidepressants and menopause treatment have different roles and should be chosen with you.
  • HRT is not a universal depression treatment, and its risks differ from those of the combined contraceptive pill.

Frequently asked questions

What is the main cause of depression around menopause?

There is no single cause. Hormonal changes can interact with sleep, previous depression, health and life pressures; a simple serotonin-deficiency explanation is inadequate.

Which symptoms should I mention?

Persistent low mood or irritability, loss of enjoyment, changes in appetite or sleep, low energy, concentration or decision difficulties, and thoughts of death or self-harm. Explain how these affect daily life.

What is the best treatment?

It depends on severity, history, risks and preferences. Talking therapy, antidepressants or both may help; appropriate menopause symptom treatment can be considered alongside depression care.

When should I see a clinician?

When symptoms affect daily activities or persist most days for about two weeks, and sooner if severe or worsening. Suicidal thoughts need urgent help; immediate danger or inability to stay safe needs emergency care.

Can I use HRT after menopause?

Sometimes, after an individual benefits-and-risks review. Postmenopause alone is not a ban, but HRT is not automatically the treatment for diagnosed depression.

Does high blood pressure rule out every hormone treatment?

No. Uncontrolled pressure needs treatment before HRT, while controlled pressure may allow an individualized plan. The combined contraceptive pill has different restrictions; never choose by this distinction alone.

Will depression end when periods stop?

Not necessarily. Some symptoms improve, but depression can persist or recur and may need ongoing treatment and relapse prevention.

Should I stop an antidepressant if I start HRT?

Do not stop or change it yourself. Review both treatments with the prescriber, including benefits, side effects, interactions and any gradual stopping plan.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
